title: Security Questionnaire Sales Acceleration: Cut Review Time
summary: Security questionnaires can stall B2B deals for weeks. Learn how to set a turnaround SLA, assign ownership and measure revenue impact, and how to speed up answers.
body_markdown:
A security questionnaire is a list of questions a buyer sends to check how a vendor protects data, and it usually arrives after the buyer is already interested. That timing is why it matters to revenue: every day the questionnaire waits in a queue is a day the deal does not move. The fastest way to speed up sales here is to treat the questionnaire as a sales stage with an owner, a target and a reusable answer base, then automate the drafting so experts only review. That is what Skypher's[Questionnaire Automation Tool](https://www.skypher.co/deprecated/security-questionnaires-automation-software) is built for.

## TL;DR


- Security review is a known source of delay: one 2026 benchmark puts it at 2 to 8 weeks for enterprise buyers, and a buyer-side roundup names it the top delay for half of enterprise buyers after selection.
- Set a security review stage in the pipeline with entry and exit criteria, an owner who is not the account executive, and a written turnaround target.
- A centralized, owned knowledge base with scheduled reviews has cut turnaround by more than 60% in a practitioner case study.
- Measure three things in your CRM: review cycle length, deals lost to security, and days to close with and without a review.
- Automation drafts answers in seconds; people stay accountable for accuracy.

## Why questionnaires slow deals down


Enterprise buyers send questionnaires (SIG Lite, CAIQ or a custom spreadsheet) before a vendor enters serious evaluation. A[cybersecurity sales-cycle benchmark from Gangly](https://getgangly.com/blog/cybersecurity-sales-cycle) says this step adds 2 to 8 weeks. It adds that a 200-person tech company may finish a review in two weeks, while a regulated healthcare or financial-services buyer can take two to four months.


The buyer side confirms the pattern. A[statistics roundup from GTM Only](https://gtmonly.com/how-b2b-buyers-use-ai/) reports IT security review as the biggest post-selection delay for 39% of buyers, and the top delay for 50% of enterprise buyers.


Two things make this worse each year:


- **Questionnaires are getting longer.** A[SprintOps Data Group study](https://hhfri.org/research/enterprise-vendor-security-requirements-2026/) of 1,200 Fortune 1000 questionnaires found the median grew from 194 questions in 2022 to 287 in 2025.
- **More people are involved.**[Forrester's buying research, as reported by Bebop](https://bebop.ai/roles/enterprise-account-executive) , finds an average of 13 internal stakeholders and 9 external participants influencing a purchase, so a security reviewer is rarely the only gatekeeper.


For a Sales Director this shows up as slipped close dates. For a CISO or GRC lead it shows up as the same question answered for the fiftieth time by someone who would rather be doing risk work.


## What it costs in revenue


The revenue effect has two parts: lost time and lost deals.


**Time.**[Revspire's customer-data benchmark](https://www.revspire.io/research/b2b-sales-objections-benchmark) (12 months to October 2026) found that deals with a security objection logged ran a median of 14 extra days, with a median discount of only 4%. In other words, the cost of security review is mostly time rather than price.


**Deals.**[KillChain Sales](https://www.killchainsales.com/blog/security-questionnaires-killing-cybersecurity-deals) reports that 54% of companies say they have lost a deal because they could not complete questionnaires on time. Gangly's benchmark also notes that deals closed within 50 days of entering the pipeline carry a 47% win rate, against roughly 20% or lower beyond that point. Treat these as directional: they come from vendor-side benchmarks, so your own CRM data is the number that counts.


The assurance behind the questionnaire matters too. The SprintOps study associates the lack of a SOC 2 Type II attestation with a median enterprise sales cycle of 8.4 months, against 5.0 months for certified vendors. A questionnaire answered quickly, with evidence attached, is how that attestation turns into speed.


If you need a business case for budget, the logic in[why third-party reviews help startups scale](https://babylovegrowth.ai/blog/why-ai-startups-trust-third-party-reviewers) applies: assurance that buyers recognize shortens the trust-building phase, and that time is what you are pricing.


## Setting a realistic turnaround SLA


A turnaround SLA (service level agreement) is an internal promise on how many business days a completed questionnaire takes from receipt to return. Without one, the work goes to whoever shouts loudest.


A[ZielLab guide for RevOps](https://ziellab.com/post/security-questionnaire-b2b-sales-revops-guide) describes the typical gap: 14 to 28 days for a full ad hoc questionnaire, against 1 to 3 days for teams with a maintained answer library. It suggests five business days as a reasonable internal target once a library exists, and ten days in the first quarter while you build it.


A practical way to set yours:


1. **Pull the last 20 questionnaires** and record receipt date, return date and number of questions.
2. **Split by type** : standard frameworks (SIG Lite, CAIQ), custom spreadsheets, portal-based forms and long due diligence questionnaires.
3. **Set tiers** , for example a shorter target for standard frameworks and a longer one for custom or portal forms with evidence requests.
4. **Publish the tiers to sales** so reps can tell the buyer a date on the first call.
5. **Review monthly** and tighten the target as the answer base matures.


The number matters less than the fact that it is written down, visible in the CRM and owned by someone.


## Build a security review stage with the right owner


The same ZielLab guide recommends a dedicated security review stage between verbal commitment and contracting. Entry criteria: the questionnaire is received and an owner is assigned. Exit criteria: answers are returned and the buyer has acknowledged them. It also argues that the account executive should not own the stage, because quota pressure pushes the work down the list the moment something more winnable appears. Ownership fits better with RevOps, a customer-facing technical person such as a solutions engineer, or the deal desk.


For defining roles and keeping the handoffs clean, the habits in[secure document sharing for contracts and sensitive files](https://learn.snappact.co/blog/secure-document-sharing) apply to the evidence you attach: send the right file, to the right person, with a record of what went out.


A workable split of responsibilities:


Role Responsibility


Solutions engineer or RevOps Owns the stage, tracks the SLA, first review of drafted answers


Security or GRC lead Approves new or changed answers, owns evidence such as policies and reports


Domain owners (IT, HR, legal, engineering) Answer questions in their area and revalidate on schedule


Account executive Tells the buyer the delivery date, escalates blockers


## Faster without losing accuracy


Speed that produces wrong answers creates audit and contract risk, so the order matters: governed content first, then speed.


An[ISC² practitioner case study](https://www.isc2.org/Insights/2025/10/streamlining-cybersecurity-reviews) describes centralizing answers in a knowledge base mapped to NIST CSF and ISO/IEC 27001, with domain owners and quarterly review cycles. Turnaround dropped by over 60%, routine questionnaires were answered in under three days, and audit findings fell. The author also stresses that automation does not replace governance: review cycles and named owners have to be built in so answers stay current.


In practice that means:


- **One source of truth.** Policies, past answers and reports live in a single place, with versions.
- **A named owner per domain.** Encryption questions go to engineering, background checks to HR.
- **A review date on every answer.** Stale answers are the main accuracy risk.
- **A confidence signal.** Reviewers should see which drafted answers are well supported and which need a human look first.

## Stop some questionnaires before they start


Not every buyer needs to send a custom list. A customizable customer-facing[Trust Center](https://skypher.co/trust-center) lets you publish your security and compliance posture where buyers can review it before they ask. Buyers who find what they need there often have fewer questions left, which shortens the stage for every deal that follows.


## Measuring the revenue impact


The[SaasDash.ai ROI framework](https://saasdash.ai/blog/trust-program-roi-deal-velocity) offers a useful measurement set. Track three baselines in your CRM:


1. **Security review cycle length:** days from questionnaire received to answers acknowledged.
2. **Deal loss rate to security:** share of lost deals where security was the logged reason.
3. **Days to close** segmented by whether the deal included a security review.


It models the value of faster cycles as roughly a deal's annual contract value divided by 365 for each day saved, plus any recovered deals. A worked example with your own numbers: if your average contract is $73,000, each day saved is worth about $200 per deal. A 14-day reduction across 30 enterprise deals a year is about $84,000 in time value, before counting any deal you would otherwise have lost. Replace those inputs with your own CRM data, and compare the quarter before and after you introduce the stage and the tooling.

## FAQ


### What is a good turnaround time for a security questionnaire?


There is no universal standard. One RevOps guide suggests five business days as an internal target once an answer library exists, and ten days during the first quarter. Set tiers by questionnaire type and review them monthly against your own data.


### Who should own the security review stage?


Not the account executive. Ownership works best with RevOps, a solutions engineer or the deal desk, with the security or GRC lead approving new answers. This keeps the work from being deprioritized when quota pressure rises.


### How do I show the revenue impact to leadership?


Track review cycle length, deals lost to security and days to close with and without a review. Convert days saved into value using contract value divided by 365 per day, then add recovered deals. Compare quarters before and after the change.


### Does automation hurt answer accuracy?


It does not have to. Accuracy comes from governed source content, named domain owners and scheduled reviews, as the ISC² case study shows. Confidence scoring helps reviewers focus on the answers that need the most attention.
